title: Gateless Barrier, Case 4: Bodhidharma Has No Beard
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, the main teaching is that death can be seen as an opportunity for awakening, using the metaphor of a cradle falling away. This idea encourages us to let go of our attachment to conventional notions and explore what lies beneath by being with questions rather than seeking answers. By embracing the mystery and uncertainty of koans, we can discover new ways of being and experience a sense of ease and clarity that transcends our ordinary perceptions.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
The fourth story in the Nomon collection really strips things down to the studs.
Our stories so far have all been relatively brief, some a little longer, but all the stories have involved some degree of interaction, interplay, connection, and a little bit of horseplay.

In the first case, Zhaozhou's Mu—excuse me—but at the same time, they're all in them somewhere, kind of in the core of the story, had a sort of a pointer pointing to a certain way of being or seeing things differently, shifting or turning somehow our understanding of the world, which starts out through culture and upbringing and whatnot a little bit off, according to the Buddhist tradition.
The Zen tradition is particularly interested in this minute, the kind of minute gradations in which we're a little off.
A famous poem that we chant once in a while says that how much we're off, good news and bad news, how much we're off is one hair's breadth.
So the good news is there's not much that we really have to change.
The bad news is how are you going to figure that out?
So anyway, they're stories and they're not stories at the same time.
They're stories and something more than stories.
The first case, Zhaozhou's Mu, pointed us towards our assumptions about the sort of inherent nature of things.
The second case, Baijiang's Fox, pointed us towards a sort of deeper understanding and more curiosity about cause and effect—what really leads to what?
We all have a sort of an opinion about that and a view, but are we, again, a little bit off.
The third case, Zhu Zhe's Finger, said something about wholeheartedness, devotion to practice, single pointedness.
In each case, there are layers of story around the central kind of point to as a way to invite us in, which we like because we like stories.
We actually think in terms of stories in most of our talk; it is actually stories.
Stories about you and me and this and that.
But the fourth case that we meet tonight, all the story is pretty well stripped away.
We can add some back, as I noticed a few translators add a little story back, but actually the Chinese is pretty clear.
It's very simple.
The fourth koan is Ho An's Western Barbarian; that is the title, and the story is barely longer than the title.
The story is, Ho An asked, "Why has the Western Barbarian no beard?"
No beard.
So that's it.
There's no set up.
There's no later he said section.
There's no monks.
There's no slaps or shouts.
Just this question: "Why has the Western Barbarian no beard?"
We've talked before about the beauty and how interesting it can be to really practice with questions.
We're so answer focused.
I want the answer to that, which leads to a lot of stuff getting done and a lot of narrowness, right?
So there's a beauty to opening to questions and studying questions and being with questions.
But maybe this question doesn't immediately have a lot of appeal.
"Why has the Western Barbarian no beard?"
A little odd.
So we met the trope of the Western Barbarian at the very end of the second story by Zhang's Fox.
Remember at the end, after all this complicated stuff about cause and effect and being born as a fox, punishment if you don't, if you're arrogant about it.
And the new by Zhang, helping the old by Zhang with the turning word and giving a funeral and a cremation for the fox body of the old guy.
And when at the end by Zhang explained what had happened, remember how he invited the head monk who had a glimmer of understanding to come forward.
And there was some degree of a ritual slap.

And at that point, the teacher at the very end, in approval, said, "I thought the Barbarian had a red beard, but here is a red-bearded Barbarian approving of his student as an exemplar of Bodhidharma."
You know, as an example of Bodhidharma, the famous first ancestor of Zhang.
But one thing that's weird here is that it would be very strange, as I understand it, in Confucian Chinese society to call somebody you respect, a great relative or ancestor, a Barbarian.
I thought it might be a little bit like calling George Washington a bumpkin.
He probably kind of was.
But we wouldn't say that.
So who is, what is this thing, this great ancestor, and why has this Western Barbarian no beard?
So some translators do insert a bit of a story.
I guess we can't help it.

Paul Reps, who did some of the first translations of Zen texts in English in, I think, the forties and fifties, translates this case as, "Hoan complained when he saw a picture of the bearded Barbarian, of the bearded Bodhidharma.
Why hasn't this fellow a beard?"
So it's very—he doesn't even have the word Barbarian.
"Hoan complained when he saw a picture of the bearded Bodhidharma.
Why hasn't this fellow a beard?"
So this was in short enough that I actually, with Google Translation help, could work it out character by character.

And this is hard to talk about since I can't read the Chinese properly, but I have been posting the notes, which includes the Chinese, on the website as Talus kindly gets the talks, the recordings up so you can look at it.
But if you're curious, the whole entire story is only, let's see, eleven characters.
The first two say the name of the teacher, Hoan.
The next character is Sed, then Western, then God, which I think is a gloss for Barbarian, then Beard.
Western Barbarian Beard.
Then it says reason, and then very, or just emphasis, and then it says no beard.
So maybe the most literal translation of this is—then it says no beard.
So maybe the most literal translation of these eleven characters might be something like "Hoan said Western Barbarian's beard missing.
No beard."
And there's an implied question there, which is why?
Weird.
What's the deal?
So now I'm little by little getting it how hard it is to translate this Chinese text.
You've got to respect the translators.
They're all doing their best, and it's no surprise, you put them side by side, they all look a little different, because so much is implied.
So how much do you assume is implied?
So this story is kind of like what the Tibetans call a pith expression, you know, the pith of the matter, just the heart of our practice.
Why are things not as they appear?
We all thought Bodhidharma has a beard.
It looks like a beard in the picture, but there's no beard.
Absolutely not.
No beard.
Why?
Or you thought you were you.
You look like you, not you.
Absolutely not you.
Why?

So kind of letting go of these conventional notions, you know, to see what's beneath or beside or within, because we've all like to really try to do our best to live on the surface of our life with a lot of precision, being very careful.
But it's just the surface.
It's all a little off.
We don't actually know very much about this teacher.
Some of them are introducing family stories about teachers that appear many, many times.
The first couple, Zhao Zhou and Bai Zhang, are that way.
But the next couple, including this one, we don't know much about Master Ho An, don't even know what years he was alive.
But we do have a poem he was supposed to have written just before he died, which is another famous kind of Zen thing to do.
Many stories like that.
And we'll all have to try this when it gets to be time.

So basically you surround yourself, you sit in zazen, full lotus preferably, you surround yourself with your students, and you get out your brush and your ink, and you write a little poem, maybe say a few words, and then you stop living, like when you're standing there.
And your posture is so good, you don't fall over either.
You just die.
And if they really respected you a lot, they embalmed you in that position.
So you never have to move again.
And you can see embalmed mummies of Chinese Zen teachers in temples in China.
It's actually true.
Probably not that many anymore, but there's some.
Quite a few were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution too, actually.
Anyway, here's his death poem.
*An iron tree in bloom.
The rooster lays an egg. 72 years.
The cradle has fallen.
An iron tree in bloom.
The rooster lays an egg. 72 years.
The cradle has fallen.*
Well, of course we know in the conventional world of surfaces that there are not iron trees, and even if there were, they wouldn't bloom.
And roosters don't lay eggs.
And 72 years.
It's not unusual, actually.
You know, average life expectancy in medieval China, I think, was maybe fifty or something.
But a lot of the Zen teachers lived a long time, according to these stories.
So it must be good for you.
This last line, "the cradle has fallen," Robert Aitken, Aitken Roshi, interprets this way.
He wrote, "Only at death do we lose the human confines of our birth."
Like only at death does the cradle really fall away.
So we're kind of like stuck in our cradle, you know.
We want everybody to feed us baby food and talk to us really nice.
And we're sort of babies.
So I'm once again struck by the aptness of a practice period theme of maturity, because we're kind of like in our cradle.
It's a nice cradle, though.
But also a death is an image for awakening in Zen.
So Zen likes to kind of mess things around a little bit.
Crude language like barbarians for people that we respect, you know, using the language of death for waking up for enlightenment.
Dying to your old self, you know, dying to your limited views.
And maybe then there's a new birth that's possible.
Only death makes room for birth.
So death is to be appreciated.
So here's a nice little bit from a modern Chinese Chan, Zen teacher, named Master Guo Jun.
But somehow, I don't know why, somehow this seems to me to speak to this case.
So Master Guo Jun, who's a little younger than me, was a disciple of Sheng Yin, a really important Chinese, modern Chinese Zen teacher.
They had big monasteries in Taiwan and around the world.
This is a book made out of talks that the younger teacher Guo Jun gave at a long retreat.
And typical of these kind of books are actually transcribed talks and the English speaking editors give them titles and arrange them and stuff.
And so the title given to this short chapter is "Floating, Floating."
Master Guo Jun says, "Swimming is like Chan.
How do you learn how to swim?
You first learn to float."
And how do you float?
You relax.
You do nothing.
It can be frustrating when you're learning to swim.
You flounder and flail.
You sink and swallow water.
When you're tense, you're no longer buoyant, though.
The more you try, the worse it gets.
Chan is called the practice of no practice.
Don't do anything and you will get it.
Babies are born with the ability to float.
They float in the wombs of their mothers.
We all want to go back to this original state.
We want to relax and float.
If you look at how Chan masters teach, they're all different.
But behind this multiplicity is a single purpose.
They use every opportunity to bring their students back to their original nature.
No fixed way.
No fixed form.
The method of no method.
All of life is teaching.
Once you try to pin it down, you make it this and not that.
What happens?
You sink.
So relax.
Be open.
Receptive.
Floating.
Chan master Zhao Zhou taught by telling people to go drink tea.
Nan Chuan challenged his monks to say one true word about a cat.
They could not.
He chopped the cat in half.
The monks were speechless.
Nan Chuan did as he had promised, but he only chopped the cat once.
He didn't make a habit of it.
Back to the violence.
The ritual violence of Zen of Chan.
Some Chan masters shout, scream, and punch.
These methods appear only once.
They can only appear once.
The method of no method.
No fixed form.
In another situation, the same Chan master will teach in a different way.
That is why we call Chan the methodless method, the gateless gate.
This is the essence and spirit of Chan.
Let's read that first paragraph again.
It's really good for us.
"Swimming is like Zen.
How do you learn how to swim?
You float.
How do you float?
You relax.
You do nothing."
So actually there are quite a few lovely little chapters, and this is a nice little book called *Essential Chan Buddhism*.
I just got a hold of this book.
It was published in two thousand ten or something like that.
Maybe I'll read some other little bits during practice period if there's time.
So what is useful or helpful, though, about a boiled down koan like "Why has the Western Barbarian no beard?"
Well, maybe I'll go ahead and tell you at least as much as I can remember the story of my first serious dip into what in the west we're calling koan introspection.
So like practicing with Mu.
Practicing in zazen and in a context with a teacher with just the pith expression.
Just this core part of the koan, which in this case, story four, there's nothing but that.
Nothing else.
It's a zazen based system which has been much written about and talked about, especially in the early books about Zen.

Very exciting and also often misinterpreted and described really weirdly, describing these stories like puzzles or problems unsolvable problems that are designed to sort of self-destruct your intellect and then out of the sort of cracked open, a new wonderful embryonic person emerges.
The cradle falls and crashes into pieces.
If you get good with your koans is the way they talked about it, which isn't totally wrong but is not at all right either.
So most often, you know, the conversations and this process around koans is held really privately because it'd be so easy to misunderstand and judge and compare and grasp and so on.
But there's also a lot of problems with secrecy, you know.
Secrets inspire us to do the exact same thing, right?
Compare, judge, assume, project, you know.
So I thought I'd tell you this little story at least a little bit of it.
It's funny trying to tell this now; it doesn't really sound that interesting.
At the time it was pretty fascinating, but now it's just kind of boring.
Before I do that, I should warn myself and you of something.
Did you know that in the early Buddhist precepts code, the Vinaya and the Pratimoksha, there's only three lapses of precepts that are serious enough to merit permanent expulsion?
All the other ones you can kind of like do penance, you know, and get back in the good graces of the Sangha and the Buddha.
There's three things that are so bad you're out forever.
The first was killing somebody.
The second was—because these were celibate orders—the second was having sex with somebody.
Actually, there's kind of graphic descriptions of what they mean by that exactly.
How far you know.
And the third, though, is the terrible precept violation of bragging about spiritual accomplishment.
So I hope I'm not going to do that.
So honestly, I honestly can't remember everything that happened in the many dokusan exchanges I had when I got to sort of study my first koan in this Rinzai kind of intense pithy way.
But here are a few impressions and highlights in case this is interesting to get a sense of something like this Western Barbarian story actually being useful, you know, not just like weird.
So exactly a year ago from now, I was on Oahu, Hawaii, at the Pololo Zendo for an eight-day rohatsu session.
Pololo Zendo was founded by Robert Aitken, the author of this wonderful book on our book of koans and his diamond sangha in the nineteen nineties.
They were previously on Maui, I think from the seventies to the early nineties.
They're on Maui, and the group actually was founded in nineteen fifty-nine.
Yeah, so this is a very early American Zen group, part of why Robert Aitken Roshi was so important in our history.

I was trying to look up what year they bought these different properties this afternoon, and an interesting fact came to my attention, though, which is that the property for these residential zendos in Hawaii was run by these small sanghas was actually completely funded by Robert Aitken's wife Anne Aiken, who had inheritance money which she gave all of it to the sangha.
So it's a little weird that I just a paragraph ago said that this zendo was founded by Robert Aitken when in fact it was bankrolled, you know, purchased by Anne Aiken.
So I'm going to try to recondition myself now that I know that to say Robert and Anne Aiken.
Anne and Robert Aitken, and she was a serious Zen student herself, completed koan studies, had important enlightenment experience.
I wrote a little book about it, which I don't know if it's available anywhere.
I struggled a lot with the patriarchal, sort of sexist nature of the thing, and I met Bob Aiken only once, but he was kind of a stern guy of his time.
I suspect he didn't give her a whole lot of room, much as he did love her very much, clearly.
I actually met him right after she died, a couple of months after she died.
It's a nice place; they have a zendo, maybe a touch bigger than this, with some sort of breezeways off of it.
Everything is open.

This is Hawaii, and there are some rooms for sleeping in and a little apartment that it was built for Robert and Anne Aiken to live in the last years of their lives, and a kitchen and a little dining room, but not so big you could fit maybe more than thirty-five or forty people max there.
At the sesshin, I found myself—I was not even at capacity; it was like twenty-five people.
Pretty much all of whom, except me and this one other woman, knew each other very, very well, like some of the people around here.
Clearly, they've been practicing together for decades and decades, because if this style of practice requires a kind of a long-term commitment, maybe even more than ours, I don't know.
The teacher there, now Michael Kieran, I found very down to earth and kind of serious, you know, serious about the style of practice that they do there that he received from Bob.
They call him Bob Aiken or Roshi, or what do you usually call him?
Mostly in the talks, he called him the old fellow.
I remember I gave a talk those cases before he said, and the old fellow was sitting right there nodding off, you know, occasionally.
Apparently, the last few years before he got too sick to come to his end, though the old fellow wouldn't have all that impulse control.
He'd come to the talks and he'd yell stuff out sort of random times.
Michael said it was pretty hard to get through the talk sometimes, you know.
You couldn't correct him, you know.
You just kind of say, "Nah, stuff like that," yeah, that's not it.
They loved him, but I think he was a pain in the butt for the last few years anyway.
The style there is completely oriented around koans; every dharma talk is on koans.
While I was there, Michael worked through eight cases in a row from a different collection than this and gave extensive backstory on every teacher's history.
He does actually know a little Chinese; he studied at the University of Hawaii, so he was explaining some of the characters and where they came from and stuff like that.
Everybody except maybe the new gal who was there has assigned to them a koan that they're studying in this pith way, koan introspection way, and everybody has dokusan with the teacher every day.
With a little bit of hustle, you can see him probably twice in a day if you want to.
There was absolutely one clear teacher there, some senior students and a head student like we have during practice period.
She made some gave some words in the zendo, but he was the only one giving interviews or doing talks, very clearly the teacher.
Michael and I had met the previous summer at a Zen teacher meeting in Portland, and I liked him and I felt comfortable, and it gave me this idea, maybe it'd be cool to go to a sesshin with him.
I don't know if I thought of like maybe he'd let me play with koans at that point, or if I thought of it later, I don't remember anyway.

I also for years had been wanting to do a little better at going to retreats where you know I get I'm just a student and maybe a different teacher, and I probably learned something, because I kind of had been doing the same style forever and mostly with one teacher.
So I did, and after initial dokusan to kind of get to know each other a little bit, I asked if it would be okay if I tried koan study, and he said okay and he assigned me a koan.

It wasn't the famous *mu*, which they often start people with; it was kind of the alternate starting place, which is a koan from Japan created a little bit after these early collections about a master of Japan named Basui.
This is another one; it's very similar to our tonight's story, that's why I thought of it.
The whole koan is:
*Basui asked who is the one who hears?*

Basui was a fourteenth-century Japanese master, so Michael gave me just a few simple instructions: turn the question over in your mind, sit with it, breathe with it, hold it close, don't push, don't try too hard, but don't slack off either.
See where it leads you, and in our daily meetings, I'll ask you about it.
I was interested in the process, so I didn't get too worked up about it or worried about it, you know, whether I was going to do a good job or a bad job.
I figured my main intention there was to just be an explorer, you know.
It's fun; it's really fun to go to a different style of Zen, you know.
You learn a lot just five minutes walking in the door and then you hang out for eight days like I did.

You learn more because they lead a very vigorous machine, so I figured my main job was just a such a sheen, you know, and I got to literally sit in the corner facing the wall, and my only job was washing the dinner dishes.
I got these luxurious breaks after breakfast and lunch.
It was just like amazing.
Everyone else took a nap, so I kind of wandered the neighborhood, hiked in the woods and stuff, but it is vigorous.
The wake-up bell goes off at four a.m., and I was warned ahead.
I guess they warn you this because they must have got a lot of complaints, but there's no coffee.
This concerned me a little to be honest, but I figured, okay, well, we'll just see.
You know what's the worst thing going to happen?
A lot of drowsiness.
But then the neat thing that I discovered the very first morning was that actually there's a whole morning routine that they do together.
It's not just, you know, sit zazen immediately after the bell goes off at four.
You're supposed to be in the zendo by four twenty, I think it was, but then the first thing they do is fast can hand we'll wake you up, warm you up, you know, that gives you some energy.
Then they gave us fifteen or twenty minutes to like stretch whatever, however we want to stretch, and people are sort of on the decks and in the zendo stretching.
Then the bell rings and you sit down in your seat, and the two servers dash out to the kitchen.

They did a lot dashing around and dash back in with a tray full of tea, big like kind of the bigger of our tea cups, filled to the brim with really good strong green tea, so there was caffeine after all, but you didn't really linger with it.
They drank it really fast, and then it was from there was pretty much the routine that we're used to here: sit, walk, sit, walk.
Meals were oriochi, pretty similar to how we do it.
Daily talks in the morning, dokusan in the afternoon, I think just all afternoon for dokusan.

Not evening, when it was time for dokusan, a special bell rang, and everybody got up, left the zendo, and sat down and kind of a line went after the next, and you go in one at a time and kind of scooch up this line.

It's kind of like this long, long mat, and then when you're in the front, you hear the bell ring out, answering bell, and you hustle back there, got a hustle, and you sit down and have a brief interview, five to ten minutes, five minutes usually, ten minutes maybe tops.

My turn came, and so I entered the room with the prostration at the door, and there's kind of a hop up under the mat in front of Michael, and without missing a beat, he asked me, "Who is the one who hears?"
Kind of a little smile, "Who is the one who hears?"
And I've been turning it over, I've been listening a lot, you know.
It seemed relevant.
It's not just a sort of an abstract object of meditation, right?
These words have meaning still.
I tried at first to go in with like zero agenda, like no plan, no answer, just see if he asked me that question what would pop out of my mouth.
One time, what popped out of my mouth was, "He is really far away."
And he kind of laughed a little, "No, he's not; he's right here."
Ring his little bell sometimes, just like in the stories.
Michael would ring his little bell, "Time to go."
Other times, we would just have this little formal exchange, two or three minutes maybe, and then we would chat a little bit, you know, have a little collegial chat, which I really appreciated.
I really felt seen, like invited to do it, right?
Invited to be a student, but also seen as a colleague, so I really appreciated Michael a lot.
But sometimes he would just ring the bell, obviously, that's off, you know.
Not even kind of after a few days, I had the intuition that although, well, it's really good to stay pretty open and not try like just see what comes up, that was a little too loose, you know.
It's a little too not engaged.
That actually, even though it probably wouldn't help to try to figure out some answer to this question, "Who's the one that hears?"
I did need to engage my intelligence.
I didn't need to show up more.

I started to kind of dance between sort of thinking about it in the dokusan room, "Who is the one that hears?" and just kind of see what words would come, and then just letting whatever words I've been sort of you know rolling around in my mind meet whatever emerged in the moment when he asked me yet again, "Who is the one who hears?"

The impressive thing is that most—I don't know how many different koans were in play, but at least twenty probably—and every single person the teacher can remember what case you're on and very directly immediately before you have time to kind of get into anything, ask you the question from your koan.
So that's impressive, and also part of why it couldn't be that big of a sesshin anyway.
So yeah, I didn't want to just be sort of spontaneous.
I realized that wasn't quite right.
It's not just about that, and besides, I was a little embarrassed by some of the wonky things that were coming out of my mouth, not even close.
So then I'm trying to kind of play with integration, you know, working with it and letting it happen.
I said something in one of the dokusons a couple days in, something I don't remember the exact words, but the spirit was something like, "He's clear as a bell."
And Michael said something like, "Well, keep exploring."

Then in one of these luxurious breaks after lunch, when I had so much free time and it was so quiet—they're really good at keeping the silence, maybe they were secretly having meetings somewhere I didn't see—but there was like, you know, we'd get it down pretty good, you know, if we have trouble with the last five percent, you know, here was like they took it down to zero, you know, there was no talking at all, so it's really peaceful.

So after lunch one time, I walked up the valley a little bit, kind of lay down in this kind of abandoned place up above and look at the sky and listen to the Hawaiian birds, which are mostly from Asia and elsewhere else, and just really listened, really listened.
I kept going back there to really listen: "Who is the one who hears?
Who is the one who hears?"
Finally, what came to me is something around it being about the one who hears needs to be present, but also needs to get out of the way.
How to hold those two, you know, to show up but not to be obstruction, not to be confusion, not to be interference with the free flow of hearing and sound, the free flow of living and dying.
So what finally came to me was, the one who hears is the one who isn't trying to be someone, the one who isn't trying to be someone.
Just felt right, you know.
Flashing lights did not go off in my mind, but it's just kind of feeling of ease with the question, like, "Oh."
I didn't have like confidence exactly, you know.
Like I was still, you know, like I was still there, you know, but I went in, I expressed that, you know, from the heart, you know, from the gut, and Michael said, "Well, that's pretty clear."
He seemed a little surprised.
He never said, "Congrats," "Good job," you know, anything like that, and he encouraged me to work with the story, the koan, a little bit longer and just see what else came up.
But he basically was saying, "Yeah, that's a good answer."
I went back the next day, and we had an interesting sort of exchange about it, like he's sort of checking me or something.
It was a beautiful little dialogue, which I can't really remember.

It was a little bit like when we do the shuso ceremony, the shosan ceremonies, like that kind of exchange, or you can't really remember later you're just speaking from the heart, but you're in this field of symbolic Zen language, you know, but it feels authentic and real.
At some point, one of those exchanges, he said something like, "You know, it's all over like space."
And I said, "No, it's right here on the ground."
And he said, "It's right here, right above your head."
And I said, "I can't reach that high," and it's just like, you know, stuff like that, which sounds ridiculous to talk about.
It felt right at the time.
Then the last day, I think this all kind of wrapped up about the sixth or seventh day.
This was eight full days actually.
Morning, night, bedtime was at nine.
He just encouraged me, "Just be with the one who hears, just appreciate your intimacy with that story, and that now this process is something that can be supportive in your life."
So, a rich experience, interesting, you know, sometimes boring, right?
This stills ozzen, you know, sometimes energizing, sometimes tiring, but essentially just pretty even.
A major punctuation, like the major sort of teacher of the sesshin, actually was there.

There's a group of wild chickens in the backyard with a cut with a rooster, and the rooster would go off before the wake of bell usually actually, so sometimes we're awake before four, but then just go off randomly, really loud, and especially he liked to to be really loud, especially during the talks, so sometimes a little hard to hear what Michael is saying because of the chickens, which I guess is a problem all over Hawaii, lots of wild chickens.
So that's my little story of Basui's who is the one who hears.
And one could practice in a very similar way with "Why is the barbarian no beard?"
You know, it's not exactly about barbarians or beards or gender or identity, but it's also not not about that, do you know what I mean?
There's something to these powerful images, you know, a powerful teacher, the barbarian from the west with his big red beard that we can drop into and explore and be moved by and engage with.

And it actually does make a certain kind of sense when you're in the middle of it, but as they say, once you write it down or talk about it later, it sounds a little weird and easily can be misinterpreted in the way it is in so many books, even books by pretty respected scholars.
Will have this whole koan study thing in this style really wrong.
